title: Why tongue twisters?
goal: Short phrases. Careful movements. Clearer speech.

study.title: Practice one difficult movement.
paragraphs: A tongue twister puts similar or difficult sounds close together. That gives your tongue, lips, jaw, and airflow a repeated coordination task.
A short, clear repetition is more useful than racing through a blurred sentence. These exercises support pronunciation; they do not replace listening and conversation.

study.title: Let your ear and mouth notice the difference.
paragraphs: Some contrasts may be unfamiliar in your first language. Right and light, road and load, or rice and lice can initially sound or feel alike.
Give the difference time and attention. This course also includes S / SH, TH / F, word endings, consonant clusters, and rhythm.
examples: Keep the contrast clear before speeding up.

study.title: A small, purposeful collection.
paragraphs: Each phrase has a target. Listen to the existing sample, notice that target, and try the phrase once or twice. You can use Practice to build it in smaller steps.

study.title: Bring the movement back to everyday words.
paragraphs: You do not need hundreds of tongue twisters. Return to a few useful patterns and then use their movements in ordinary phrases.
Listen, notice, and try. When you feel comfortable, practice L and R in one short sentence in the next lesson.
